'''John Kenneth Truss''' (born April 1947) is an English mathematician. He is an [[emeritus professor]] of [[pure mathematics]] at the [[University of Leeds]] where he specialises in [[mathematical logic]], infinite [[permutation group]]s, homogeneous structures and [[model theory]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://eps.leeds.ac.uk/maths/staff/4087/professor-j-k-truss |title=Professor J K Truss &#124; School of Mathematics &#124; University of Leeds |website=eps.leeds.ac.uk |access-date=7 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220223210547/https://eps.leeds.ac.uk/maths/staff/4087/professor-j-k-truss |archive-date=23 February 2022 |url-status=dead}}</ref> Truss began his career as a junior research fellow at the [[University of Oxford]] before holding a series of academic positions and lastly joining the University of Leeds. He has written books on discrete mathematics (1991) and mathematical analysis (1997) and was co-editor in chief of the ''[[Journal of the London Mathematical Society]]'' until June 2003. He is the father of the former [[Prime Minister of the United Kingdom]], [[Liz Truss]].

==Early life and family==
John Truss was born in April 1947.<ref>[https://id.loc.gov/authorities/names/nr88008393.html Truss, J. K.], Library of Congress. Retrieved 15 September 2022.</ref><ref>[https://viaf.org/processed/CAOONL|ncf10980382 Virtual International Authority File.] Retrieved 15 September 2022.</ref> He graduated from [[King's College, Cambridge]], in 1968 and earned his PhD at the University of Leeds in 1973 for a dissertation titled "Some Results about Cardinal Numbers without the Axiom of Choice" which was supervised by Frank Drake.<ref>[https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=82577 John Kenneth Truss.] Mathematics Genealogy Project. Retrieved 12 September 2022.</ref> In 1969, he married Priscilla Mary Grasby, a nurse,<ref name="Grylls">{{Cite news |first1=Andrew |last1=Norfolk |first2=Charlotte |last2=Wace |first3=George |last3=Grylls |title=Liz Truss: from teenage Lib Dem to darling of the Tory right |newspaper=[[The Times]] |language=en |url=https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/article/liz-truss-profile-parents-family-school-kcxznq2wb |url-access=subscription |access-date=7 September 2022 |issn=0140-0460}}</ref> who he had met while they were students at Cambridge.<ref name="Grylls" /> Together, they have a daughter, [[Liz Truss]], and three sons.<ref name="LTBS_1">{{cite web |author1=Josh Glancy |author2=Hugo Daniel |date=3 September 2022 |title=Just where is Liz Truss from? Her incredible journey spans three countries and two continents |url=https://www.thetimes.com/article/22ba44e0-2b98-11ed-b39f-ae396665d39a?shareToken=88fac60348b32bb7bb5a9daf34142dd0 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220904065449/https://www.thetimes.co.uk/article/22ba44e0-2b98-11ed-b39f-ae396665d39a?shareToken=88fac60348b32bb7bb5a9daf34142dd0 |archive-date=4 September 2022 |access-date=6 September 2022 |work=[[The Times]]}}</ref> Liz Truss has described her parents' politics as "to the left of [[Labour Party (UK)|Labour]]".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Quinn |first=Ben |date=5 September 2022 |title=How Liz Truss became leader of the Conservative party – a timeline |url=https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2022/sep/05/liz-truss-leader-conservative-party-timeline |website=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> Truss and his wife were both supporters of the [[Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2022-09-06/who-is-liz-truss-britains-next-prime-minister/101404932 |title=How Liz Truss, Britain's next prime minister, went from anti-monarchist rebel to the next Margaret Thatcher|first=Jack |last=Hawke |publisher=[[ABC News (Australia)|ABC News]] |date=5 September 2022 |access-date=14 March 2023}}</ref> They divorced in 2003.<ref name="Grylls" />

Truss refused to campaign with his daughter on her selection for [[Conservative Party UK|Conservative]] candidate for [[South West Norfolk]] in the [[2010 UK general election]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Cole |first1=Harry |title=[[Out of the Blue: The Inside Story of the Unexpected Rise and Rapid Fall of Liz Truss]] |last2=Heale |first2=James |date=2022 |publisher=[[HarperCollins]] |isbn=978-0-00-860578-0 |author-link1=Harry Cole (journalist)}}</ref>

==Career==
Truss's first academic position was as a junior research fellow at the [[Mathematical Institute]] of the University of Oxford.<ref>"Models of set theory containing many perfect sets", ''Ann. Math. Logic'' 7, 197–219 (1974).</ref> He then taught at a school in [[Kidderminster]],<ref>[https://www.oxfordmail.co.uk/news/20994953.oxford-liz-truss/ Where in Oxford is Liz Truss from?] Miranda Norris, ''Oxford Mail'', 6 September 2022. Retrieved 12 September 2022.</ref> Worcestershire, before lecturing at [[Paisley College of Technology]] from 1979 to 1985.<ref name="Grylls" /> In 1987, he worked at [[Simon Fraser University]]<ref>{{Cite web |last=Chan |first=Cheryl |date=6 September 2022 |title=New U.K. prime minister Liz Truss attended school in Burnaby |url=https://vancouversun.com/news/local-news/uk-prime-minister-liz-truss-school-burnaby |access-date=6 September 2022 |website=[[Vancouver Sun]] |language=en-CA}}</ref> in British Columbia, Canada, and later at the University of Leeds where in 1988 with Frank Drake he edited the collected papers of Logic Colloquium '86, held at the [[University of Hull]] in 1986.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Skowron |first=Andrzej |date=1989 |title=Review of Logic Colloquium '86 |journal=Studia Logica |volume=48 |issue=3 |pages=396–400 |issn=0039-3215 |jstor=20015451}}</ref>

In 1990, [[Peter Cameron (mathematician)|Peter Cameron]] paid tribute to Truss in his notes on ''Oligomorphic Permutation Groups'' in the London Mathematical Society Lecture Notes Series No. 152, for saving him from "making some rash [[conjecture]]s (by disproving them)", and "notably" for his contribution to the question of what are the possible cycle structures of [[automorphisms]] of ''M''?<ref>Cameron, Peter J. (1990). ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=ZV9Md1BvlWkC&dq=truss&pg=PA3 Oligomorphic Permutation Groups]''. London Mathematical Society Lecture Notes Series No. 152. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press. pp. v, 3, 86, 104. ISBN 0-521-38836-8</ref> In 1991, Truss published ''Discrete Mathematics for Computer Scientists'' which [[John Bayliss (mathematician)|John Bayliss]] described in ''[[The Mathematical Gazette]]'' as "masterful and thorough" and getting "rapidly to the heart of some very exciting topics" but felt that it was more of a mathematician's book than a book for computer scientists as claimed by the author. Nonetheless, Bayliss felt that the approach taken by Truss in organising and presenting his material was highly successful in condensing different strands of mathematics so that the author had shown that "[[discrete mathematics]] has come of age and is no longer a collection of disparate topics."<ref name="Baylis-1992">{{Cite journal |last=Baylis |first=John |date=1992 |title=Review of Discrete Mathematics for Computer Scientists |journal=[[The Mathematical Gazette]] |volume=76 |issue=476 |pages=303–305 |doi=10.2307/3619163 |issn=0025-5572 |jstor=3619163}}</ref>

In 1999, Truss and [[S. Barry Cooper]], also of the University of Leeds, jointly edited two volumes of papers in the [[London Mathematical Society Lecture Notes Series]] arising from the European meeting of the [[Association for Symbolic Logic]] in Leeds in July 1997 on sets and proofs<ref name="Priest-2001">{{Cite journal |last=Priest |first=Graham |author-link=Graham Priest |date=2001 |title=Review of Sets and Proofs; Models and Computability, S. Barry Cooper, John K. Truss |journal=[[Studia Logica]] |volume=69 |issue=3 |pages=446–448 |issn=0039-3215 |jstor=20016368}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cantini |first=Andrea |date=2002 |title=Review of First Steps into Metapredicativity in Explicit Mathematics |journal=[[The Bulletin of Symbolic Logic]] |volume=8 |issue=4 |pages=535–536 |doi=10.2307/797965 |issn=1079-8986 |jstor=797965}}</ref> and models and computability.<ref name="Priest-2001" /> The volumes were welcomed by philosopher [[Graham Priest]] of the [[University of Queensland]] who noted that they concentrated on logic as practiced in mathematics departments with little content of a philosophical or computer science nature, but, possibly as a result, were more coherent than usual for collections of conference papers.<ref name="Priest-2001"/> By then, Truss and [[Jonathan Partington]] were co-editors of the ''[[Journal of the London Mathematical Society]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |url=http://www2.cup.cam.ac.uk/scripts/webjrn1.asp?mnemonic=jlm |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19990913212836/http://www2.cup.cam.ac.uk/scripts/webjrn1.asp?mnemonic=jlm |archive-date=13 September 1999}}</ref> They were succeeded on 6 June 2003 by [[Francis Burstall]] and [[John Toland (mathematician)|John Toland]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |url=http://www1.maths.leeds.ac.uk/~pmt6jrp/jlms/index.html |access-date=6 September 2022 |website=www1.maths.leeds.ac.uk}}</ref>
